bio.en: Julian Shapiro is the founder of Demand Curve, a growth-training company that has helped thousands of startups with their growth strategy, and previously wrote the growth column at TechCrunch and led marketing at Webflow.
bio.zh: 朱利安·夏皮罗（Julian Shapiro）是增长培训公司 Demand Curve 的创始人，已帮助数千家初创公司制定增长战略；他此前曾为 TechCrunch 撰写增长专栏，并担任 Webflow 的市场营销副总裁。

summary.en: Julian makes the case for product-led acquisition (PLA) as the most durable and capital-efficient way to grow a company. He shares concrete tactics for improving retention and a framework for producing novel, engaging content, including the "Curiosity Faucet" creativity method. The episode also covers how to pick topics and write in a way that earns attention.
summary.zh: 朱利安主张"产品驱动获取"（PLA）是公司最持久、最具资金效率的增长方式。他分享了提升留存的具体策略，以及创作新颖、有吸引力内容的框架，包括"好奇心水龙头"这一激发创造力的方法。本期还涉及如何选题，以及如何写出真正能赢得注意力的内容。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Why do good ideas arrive after the bad ideas are empty? It's because when you've gone through a bunch of bad ideas, your brain, your mind starts reflexively identifying what elements are causing the badness. Then it becomes way better at avoiding those bad elements and you become way better at pattern matching the novel ideas with way greater intuition. Most creators are resisting their bad ideas. If you sat down, scribbled a few thoughts in a blank document and just walked away because you weren't struck with gold, then you never actually finished the creative process. There's no way you would've come up with gold.
turns.zh: 为什么好点子总是在坏点子被否定后才涌现？这是因为当你经历了一堆坏点子后，大脑会自动识别导致失败的因素，从而更善于规避这些负面因素，也能更敏锐地将新奇想法与直觉相匹配。大多数创作者都抗拒自己的坏点子。如果你只是在空白文档里随便写几句想法，然后因为灵感枯竭就放弃，那你永远无法完成创作过程，也不可能产出优秀的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Welcome to Lenny's Podcast. I'm Lenny, and my goal here is to help you get better at the craft of building and growing products. I interview world class product leaders, and growth experts to learn from their hard-won experiences building and scaling today's most successful companies today. My guest is Julian Shapiro. I actually spend a bunch of time introducing the wondrous Julian at the beginning of the episode. Instead, let me just share some of the things that we talk about. We get into a framework he calls product-led acquisition, which is work that has come out of his working with thousands of companies, helping to figure out their growth strategies.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到Lenny的播客。我是Lenny，我的目标是帮助你提升产品打造和增长的技能。我会采访世界级的产品领袖和增长专家，从他们成功打造和扩张当今最成功公司的经验中汲取智慧。本期嘉宾是朱利安·夏皮罗。通常我在节目开头会花大量时间介绍这位了不起的嘉宾，但这次我想直接分享我们讨论的内容。我们探讨了一个他称为“产品主导型获客”的框架——这个框架源于他与数千家公司合作，帮助他们制定增长策略的经验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We get into ways to increase your product's retention. Then we talk a lot about writing, the importance of novelty in your writing, how to choose a topic when you plan to write, and then a framework that Julian calls the Creativity Faucet. Julian is such a fascinating human, and I'm really excited to bring you this episode. With that, I bring you Julian Shapiro. I'm excited to chat with my friend John Cutler from podcast sponsor Amplitude. Hey, John.
turns.zh: 我们还讨论了如何提高产品的用户留存率。接着深入探讨了写作技巧、新奇性的重要性、选题策略，以及朱利安称为“创造力水龙头”的框架。朱利安非常有趣，我很兴奋能为大家带来这期播客。接下来有请朱利安·夏皮罗。我还很高兴能与播客赞助商Amplitude的约翰·卡特勒交流。约翰，你好。

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Hey, Lenny. Excited to be here.
turns.zh: 你好，Lenny。很高兴能来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: John, give us a behind the scenes at Amplitude. When most people think of Amplitude, they think of product analytics. But now you're getting into experimentation and even just launched a CDP. What's the thought process there?
turns.zh: 约翰，请给我们介绍一下Amplitude的幕后故事。当大多数人想到Amplitude时，他们会联想到产品分析。但现在你们正涉足实验领域，甚至刚刚推出了CDP。背后的思考逻辑是什么？

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Well, we've always thought of Amplitude as being about supporting the full product loop. Think collect data, inform that, ship experiments, and learn. That's the heart of growth to us. The big aha was seeing how many customers we're using Amplitude to analyze experiments, use segments for outreach, and send data to other destinations. Experiment in CDP came out of listening to and observing our customers.
turns.zh: 我们一直认为Amplitude的核心使命是支持完整的产品闭环：收集数据、分析数据、开展实验并从中学习。这对我们来说是增长的核心所在。最重要的启发是看到许多客户用Amplitude分析实验、使用细分客户群开展外联活动，并将数据传送至其他平台。CDP中的实验功能源于我们倾听和观察客户需求的过程中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Supporting growth and learning has always been Amplitude's core focus, right?
turns.zh: 支持增长和学习一直是Amplitude的核心关注点，对吧？

turns.speaker: John Cutler
turns.en: Yeah. Amplitude tries to meet customers where they are. We just launched starter templates and have a great scholarship program for startups. There's never been a more important time for growth.
turns.zh: 是的。Amplitude致力于贴近客户需求。我们刚刚推出了入门模板，并为初创公司设立了优秀奖学金项目。当下正是增长最为重要的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely agree. Thanks for joining us, John, and head to Amplitude.com to get started. Hey, Ashley, head of marketing and Flatfile. How many B2B SaaS companies would you estimate need to import CSV files from their customers?
turns.zh: 完全赞同。感谢约翰加入我们，有需要的请访问Amplitude.com。嘿，Ashley，市场营销负责人兼Flatfile创始人。你估计有多少B2B SaaS公司需要从客户导入CSV文件？

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.en: At least 40%.
turns.zh: 至少40%的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How many of them screw that up and what happens when they do?
turns.zh: 其中有多少公司做得一团糟？他们出错时会怎样？

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.en: Well? Based on our data, about a third of people will consider switching to another company after just one bad experience during onboarding. If your CSV importer doesn't work right, which is super common, considering customer files are chock- full of unexpected data and formatting, they'll leave.
turns.zh: 嗯？根据我们的数据，约三分之一的人在入职过程中只要有一次糟糕的体验，就会考虑跳槽到其他公司。如果你的CSV导入器出了问题——这情况很常见，毕竟客户文件里经常充斥着意外的数据和格式问题——他们就会离开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am 0% surprised to hear that. I've consistently seen that improving onboarding is one of the highest leverage opportunities for both signup conversion and increasing long-term retention. Getting people to your aha moment more quickly and reliably is so incredibly important.
turns.zh: 听到这个我一点也不惊讶。我一直认为，优化入职体验是提升注册转化率和增强长期客户留存率的最高效手段之一。让用户更快、更可靠地获得"顿悟时刻"，这一点至关重要。

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.en: Totally. It's incredible to see how our customers like Square, Spotify, and Zuora are able to grow their businesses on top of Flatfile. It's because flawless data onboarding acts like a catalyst to get them and their customers where they need to go faster.
turns.zh: 完全同意。看到我们的客户Square、Spotify和Zuora能在Flatfile平台上发展业务，真是令人惊叹。这是因为无缝的数据入职流程就像催化剂，帮助他们和客户更快达成目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you'd like to learn more or get started, check out flat file at flatfile.com/lenny. Julian Shapiro is what I'd call a polymath of the internet. He's an amazing writer, marketer and growth mind, investor, community builder, podcaster, tweeter. He's also an expert on building muscle. He's maybe most known for being the founder of Demand Curve, a YC startup that trains people on growth and marketing. Prior to that, he was a part-time columnist at TechCrunch. He was also VP of marketing at Webflow, which I had no idea about.
turns.zh: 如果您想了解更多信息或立即开始，可以访问flatfile.com/lenny。朱利安·夏皮罗在我眼中是互联网全才。他是出色的作家、营销人，具有成长思维；是投资人、社区建设者、播客主、推特达人；还是肌肉训练专家。他最广为人知的身份或许是Demand Curve的创始人，这家YC初创公司专注于增长和营销培训。在此之前，他曾是TechCrunch的兼职专栏作家，还担任过Webflow的营销副总裁（我之前对此毫不知情）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He also created a JavaScript web animation engine that is used by Uber and WhatsApp and Samsung and thousands of companies. Currently he is a full-time investor with his own fund and as a partner at Hyper. He's also one of the most hilarious and generous humans that I know. With that, Julian, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 他还开发了一个JavaScript动画引擎，Uber、WhatsApp、三星等数千家公司都在使用。目前，他全职担任投资人，管理自己的基金，并在Hyper担任合伙人。他也是我认识的最幽默、最慷慨的人之一。朱利安，欢迎做客播客。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: This is the greatest honor of my life. Thank you.
turns.zh: 这是我人生中最大的荣誉。谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow!
turns.zh: 哇！

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I'm crying from that intro. Very nice of you.
turns.zh: 听完你的开场白，我都感动哭了。你真是太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's the idea. This is the greatest honor of my life. We match.
turns.zh: 这才是重点。这是我人生中最大的荣誉。我们太合拍了。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Excellent. We'll cancel each other out and we'll see how interesting this is.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们可以相互借鉴，看看这会多有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. There's a lot of hype. I know you have something like 250,000 Twitter followers. You're very good at Twitter, but I've noticed that you've only tweeted three times this past year. What is going on there?
turns.zh: 没错。现在有很多炒作。我知道你有25万推特粉丝。你很擅长推特，但我注意到过去一年你只发了三次推文。这是怎么回事？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: There's a few things in parallel. One is a lot of people are writing threads and I found this to be very cringe. They're like these fortune cookie threads like here's 21 ways to rework your startup or something. I found them all cringe. What they actually do when you write that stuff is they attract people who think that's valuable information, and then they cause people who you actually want to follow you to unfollow you. I remember just seeing people unfollow me early days of threads when no one was doing them and I was experimenting. They were pissing off people that I actually cared to have dialogue with.
turns.zh: 有几个原因同时起作用。首先，很多人在发长文，我觉得特别尴尬。比如“21种重构创业公司的方法”之类的，我觉得都很无聊。发这种内容的结果就是吸引那些认为这是有价值信息的人，然后导致你真正想关注的人取消关注。我记得早期发长文时，没有人这样做，我只是在尝试，结果发现有人取消关注我。这真的很让人生气，因为我其实很想和那些人交流。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I kind of lost the momentum and enthusiasm for writing that sort of stuff. And now I'm only writing anything when it's basically a reflection or a condensed version of a blog post that I happen to be writing from my website. I know it's high quality. I know it's original. I know it's thoughtful. It's not for the click bait. That was part of it. The other thing is that it's kind of like too... Here's a mental model for thinking about the quality of your followers. You have people who follow you for the quality of your brain, and you have people who follow you for sort of you being a glorified curator. If they're following you for being a curator, they're sort of what I call labor followers.
turns.zh: 我有点失去了写这类内容的势头和热情。现在我写东西的时候，基本上都是把我在网站上写的博客文章进行提炼或浓缩。我知道这些内容质量很高，很有原创性，也很具思想深度。但这不是为了吸引点击量。这只是问题的一部分。另一个问题是，人们追随你，有时只是因为你是个优秀的信息整合者——我称之为"劳力型追随者"。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: They're following you for the work that you're doing, where you're finding cool, funny memes. You're posting cool, funny jokes. You're doing these fortune cookie threads. In contrast, if they're following you for your mind, which is category one, it means they're following you for the original thoughts and insights and takes that you have on the world. Someone like Paul Graham, the founder of Y Combinator, is doing original takes. He's not trying to write threads for the sake of gaining followers. He's trying to write interesting novel ideas. When he does that, he strengthens the affinity that his followers have for him and his mind, because like, "Wow! That was an original interesting take."
turns.zh: 他们追随你，是为了你所做的工作——比如寻找有趣的梗图，发布搞笑段子，开展"幸运饼干"话题讨论。相比之下，如果人们是因为你的思想而追随你（第一类），那就意味着他们欣赏你对世界独到的见解和深刻洞察。比如Y Combinator创始人保罗·格雷厄姆（Paul Graham），他总是提出原创观点。他的目的是分享有趣的新想法，而不是为了涨粉。他这样做能增强追随者对他的信任感，因为人们会感叹："哇！这真是独到的新见解！"

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: They're following you for your mind, not for the labor you're doing, putting together a virtual Buzzfeed to count on Twitter. When people follow you for your mind, when they're mind followers, not labor followers, higher affinity means more loyalty, means they pay closer attention to what you're saying. And if you actually try to get them to do something with you, you have an event offline, there's something you're selling, there's a cause you care about, they're way more likely to indulge.
turns.zh: 他们追随的是你的思想，而不是你收集梗图、在Twitter上拼凑虚拟Buzzfeed内容的劳力行为。当人们因为你的思想而追随你时，他们是"思想追随者"而非"劳力追随者"。更高的亲近感意味着更强的忠诚度，他们会更认真倾听你的观点。当你试图让他们参与某项活动、线下活动、销售产品或支持公益事业时，他们的参与意愿会高得多。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Whereas if they're following you for your labor, you're interchangeable with all these other meme accounts and there's no real affinity for you as the individual. I just care more about the quality of the follower than I do the volume.
turns.zh: 相比之下，如果人们只是为了你的劳力价值而追随你，他们就会把你和其他梗图账号混为一谈，根本没有对你个人的认可。我更关注追随者的质量而非数量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. That's such a good reminder, not to just focus on follower, follower, follower. I'm curious if someone... You have a lot of followers at this point and it's just so valuable to have Twitter followers. I've learned for me, anytime I have a question about anything, I just ask and I get so many amazing answers from people. There's this power to having a large following. I'm curious while we're on this topic, if you're just starting out on Twitter, do you have any advice for someone that's just thinking about building their following?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个观点。这是个很好的提醒，不能只关注粉丝数量。我很好奇，你现在已经有大量粉丝了，Twitter粉丝的价值确实很高。我发现，每当我有疑问时，只要发问就能得到很多精彩的回答。拥有大量粉丝确实有其力量。既然我们聊到这个话题，如果你是Twitter新手，有什么建议给那些正考虑建立粉丝基础的人吗？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I mean, generally speaking, threads, despite everything I've said, are the primary way to get followers. There's a reason why people do threads as opposed to single tweets is because when people get exposure to a thread, they're basically getting exposure to the length of thoughts equivalent to you having sent a newsletter edition or a blog post in many cases. The more exposure, the more surface area you have, the more you give people of your brain in a single tweet, the more they're able to confirm that what you're sharing is actually a consistency from you.
turns.zh: 总的来说，尽管我说了这么多，但线程仍然是获取粉丝的主要方式。人们选择发布线程而非单条推文的原因在于，当人们接触到一个线程时，他们实际上接触到的思想深度相当于你发送一期新闻通讯或一篇博客文章。在Twitter上，曝光度越高，你的思想呈现面越广，一条推文中传递的思想越多，人们就越能确认你分享的内容确实是你的个人风格。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Whereas if you just tweet one clever thing, they're like, "Oh, that's probably just a drop in the bucket. Who knows if that person can consistently generate clever stuff?" But in a long thread where it's 30 tweets and they're all good, they're like, "Whoa! This person is a machine. If I follow them reliably, I'll get more great stuff." It reaffirms to readers they should follow you, which is why threads trigger more follows. Basically you do want to do threads, frankly, and that's the backbone of it. Threads with very clickbaity opening tweets kind of how it works.
turns.zh: 相反，如果你只发一条聪明的推文，他们可能会觉得：“哦，这不过是沧海一粟罢了。谁知道这个人能否持续产出优质内容呢？” 但如果是一篇长篇推文，包含30条优质推文，他们就会惊叹：“哇！这人简直是个创作机器。如果我持续关注他们，肯定能收获更多精彩内容。” 这会让读者再次确认应该关注你，这就是长篇推文能吸引更多关注的原因。说实话，你确实应该多发长篇推文，这才是核心策略。那种标题吸引眼球的开篇推文效果尤其显著。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: You can also port followers over from other places like your website and newsletter, just to start giving yourself an initial sample audience through which the threads can actually take fire pretty much.
turns.zh: 你还可以从其他平台（比如你的网站和新闻通讯）引流粉丝，迅速为自己建立初始受众群体，助推推文热度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I wasn't expecting to go into Twitter as strategy, but this is interesting because you're really good at it. As you've said, your stuff is actually very thoughtful. It's not just a thirsty Twitter thread trying to find followers and retweets. Thanks for sharing that.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我原本没想到会聊Twitter策略，但这很有趣，因为你在这方面确实很在行。正如你所说，你的内容确实很有深度。不只是为了吸引粉丝和转发而拼命发推文的那些低级玩法。感谢分享这些心得。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Well, it sort of started that way, because me and a few other friends of mine, I felt like we were the first people doing threads at scale. And then when we realized what it turned into, that's when we just stopped.
turns.zh: 嗯，刚开始确实是那样，因为我和几个朋友觉得我们是首批大规模玩转推文的人。后来意识到这变成什么样子后，我们就停止了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I know what you mean about these cringy Twitter threads. Anyway, what I want to do is instead of asking a bunch of random questions is to focus on five big topics and kind of go deep on these topics. These are topics that are maybe most popular of the stuff that you've put out across your handbooks and writing and courses and things like that and also things that I've found to be most interesting. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你的这个想法。我懂你说的那些尴尬推文的意思。不管怎样，我想做的是，不再随意提问，而是聚焦五个核心话题，深入探讨这些主题。这些主题可能是你发布的手册、文章、课程等内容中最受欢迎的，也是我个人最感兴趣的。你觉得这样行吗？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Yeah, I would love to.
turns.zh: 好啊，我很乐意参与。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. First, a little context, you write these super in depth handbooks on a bunch of different topics on growth and writing and muscle building and things like that. First of all, could you just explain what these handbooks are and why you create them?
turns.zh: 太好了。首先，简单介绍一下背景。你写了大量关于成长、写作、肌肉训练等不同主题的深度手册。首先，能否解释一下这些手册的意义，以及你创作它们的初衷？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: They're forcing functions for me to hold myself accountable and to be thorough when learning something for my own benefit. That's all they are. Basically if I want to go learn growth or writing well or some other topic, I will go ahead and do a ton of research, read everything I can get my hands on, do a ton of experimentation to try to build a set of novel insights that you couldn't find from other people's research hopefully, and then the next stage is try to make it as concise and actionable as possible so that I can reference it for my own selfish benefit. Here's my guidebook for myself on writing better blog posts, for example.
turns.zh: 它们是我的自我约束机制，让我在学习过程中保持专注和系统性。仅此而已。比如，如果我想深入研究增长黑客、写作技巧或其他领域，我会先进行大量研究，阅读所有相关资料，进行大量实验，试图形成一些希望他人无法通过现有研究获得的新见解。然后再把这些内容尽可能简洁易行，这样我就能为自己所用了。比如，我写的关于如何写出优质博客文章的指南。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: And then by the time I've done that work, what usually happens is its only like, I'm going to make up a number here, an extra 30 hours of work to make it palatable and digestible for the public. If I've done all this work privately, why not make it accessible publicly? At that point, it winds up being acquisition fodder for essentially building an audience and distributing my thoughts further. That's why I do that. But the thing that I pride myself on with them is by no means are they thoroughly unique, but in every one there's a lot of original stuff folks on average have never heard of before.
turns.zh: 然后，当我完成这些工作后，通常会出现这样的情况：我需要额外投入30个小时的工作量，才能让内容更易于公众理解和接受。如果我已经私下完成了所有这些工作，为什么不把它公之于众呢？这样一来，它最终就会成为吸引受众、进一步传播我思想的素材。这就是我这样做的原因。但我引以为傲的是，我的作品绝非独树一帜，但每篇文章中都包含大量普通人从未听说过的原创内容。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: And that's what I'm proud of, is coming up with those insights between the lines that make that thing, whatever the topic is, much more approachable. I've succeeded, in my view, if I've made something that people often mistakenly think of as overwhelmingly complex very simple for them to follow. I think that's where the dopamine hit comes from for them.
turns.zh: 这正是我引以为傲的地方——能够挖掘出那些隐藏在字里行间的洞见，让无论主题如何，都更易于人们理解。在我看来，如果我能把那些被误认为极其复杂的内容变得简单易懂，那就是成功了。我认为，这正是能让读者获得多巴胺奖励的关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, my experience, you definitely hit the nail in my head with the handbooks you put out. It's an interesting middle ground between a newsletter and a book. It's cool to just have a digital way of doing that, of just kind of consolidating a bunch of ideas and going really in depth, but not having to write a book. Well, speaking of the contract there.
turns.zh: 嗯，以我的经验来说，你推出的那些手册确实切中了我的需求。它处于新闻通讯和书籍之间的有趣中间地带。通过数字化方式将大量想法整合并深入探讨，同时无需写成书籍，这种方式很棒。嗯，说到合同的事儿。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: You have a very large newsletter that goes very in depth. That arguably is a more valuable asset than my handbooks for someone building an audience, because the newsletter has this built-in form of retention recurrence, where they get pinged in their inbox when you have new content, and then it becomes a referable thing and people refer each other and then they sign up for the newsletter. I do love the emphasis on longform via newsletter, but the reason I do it on the web is, and we'll talk about the trade-offs in a second, is it's much more digestible and referencable.
turns.zh: 你有一份内容极其深入的大型新闻通讯。对于那些正在积累受众的人来说，它可能比我的手册更有价值，因为新闻通讯内置了用户留存和重复访问机制。当你有新内容时，它们会自动发送到用户收件箱，进而成为可被推荐的内容，人们会相互推荐，最终订阅你的新闻通讯。我确实很看重通过新闻通讯进行长篇创作，但我在网上的做法（我们稍后会讨论其中的权衡利弊）在于，它更易于理解和传播。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: No one's going to go refer to the epic guide in their email inbox that's very hard to navigate for building muscle or something. One, it's a UX decision. Two, I get the SEO traffic, which you don't. And then three, it's basically a living asset that I can keep updating over time. It's not stuck in someone's inbox and getting printed out. One of the things that might separate me from other writers, at least many other writers online, is I'm spending as many hours going back and rewriting old blog posts and handbooks as I am writing ones.
turns.zh: 没人会去在邮箱收件箱里翻找那种很难导航的关于增肌之类的巨型指南。一来，这是用户体验方面的考量；二来，我能获得SEO流量，而你却得不到；三来，这基本上是一项可以随时更新的动态资产，不会被困在用户收件箱里打印出来。我与其他作者（至少是许多在线作者）的不同之处之一在于，我花费同样多的时间回顾和重写旧博文及手册，就像写新博文一样。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: If you come back to anything I've written over the course of a year or year and a half, it'll be updated, because I consider everything I write to be evergreen. I avoid writing things that I feel like are a drop in the pan, just like talking about a trend or something, something very newsy. I avoid that altogether and I'm just interested in writing stuff that'll be relevant for a long time.
turns.zh: 如果你回看我过去一年或一年半内写的任何内容，它都会被更新，因为我认为我写的所有内容都是永不过时的。我避免写那些我觉得是昙花一现的东西，比如谈论某个趋势或新奇事物。我完全避开这些，只专注于写出能长期保持相关性的内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't know that. That is very cool. I love that you do that. You should make that clear. That's so interesting that this is not stale. Last updated, last week. I don't know if you already do that.
turns.zh: 我不知道这一点。太酷了。我喜欢你这样做。你应该把这一点明确表达出来。内容不陈旧，这太有趣了。上周更新过。我不知道你是否已经这样做了。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Yeah, no, I actually don't and I probably should. People have complained to me that I haven't, so maybe I will one day.
turns.zh: 是的，不，我实际上没有这样做，或许我应该这么做。有人向我抱怨我没有这么做，所以也许有一天我会这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. We got a good idea out of this, if nothing else.
turns.zh: 好的。即便没有别的收获，我们也从中获得了一个不错的启发。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 就这样吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. The first idea that I want to chat about is something that you call product-led acquisition. I believe it's the most popular page in any of your handbooks. It comes from you working with thousands of companies to help them figure out their growth strategies through Demand Curve. I'm curious to hear what this concept is and how people can use it to help their products grow.
turns.zh: 好的。我想先聊聊你们手册中最受欢迎的概念——“产品主导型获客策略”。这个概念源自你们通过Demand Curve帮助数千家公司制定增长策略的实践经验。我很想听听这个概念的内涵，以及如何借助它来推动产品增长。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Product-led acquisition to your audience will be more commonly known as product-led growth, but I think product-led growth is a bit of a misnomer. It's often used, as you know, to basically refer to SaaS companies who are using self-serve sales funnels where a salesperson isn't required, right? Bypassing sales and allowing the product to grow itself. That's fine. But I think the term we really care about as growth marketers is product-led acquisition, meaning the use of the product grows the product. For example, if I'm using PayPal and I'm sending $1,000 to somebody else, there is no way they will not create a PayPal account to accept the $1,000.
turns.zh:
对于听众来说，“产品主导型增长”可能更耳熟，但我认为这个术语有些误导。正如大家所知，这个术语通常指SaaS公司通过自助式销售漏斗实现增长，无需人工销售——即绕过销售环节，让产品自行发展。这没问题。但作为增长营销人员，我们真正关注的应是“产品主导型获客策略”，即通过产品自身的增长来推动产品发展。

例如，当我使用PayPal向他人转账1000美元时，对方必然会创建PayPal账户来接收这笔款项。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: By me trying to use PayPal in its everyday intention and me getting value out of it to settle a debt, I'm automatically enticing someone else, very strongly so, to also become a PayPal customer. That's product-led acquisition. There's a few different categories I've identified, and I think the reason why people like this part of this article I wrote is because it's, in my opinion, the absolute best way to grow any startup. If your startup can grow via product-led acquisition, not all can, maybe some are enterprise-base and all they're going to make work is sales, then it is by far the best way to grow because zero marginal cost to have users invite other users.
turns.zh: 我仅以PayPal为例。若我按照其日常使用场景行事，并从中获得价值（比如结清债务），我就能极大地吸引他人也成为PayPal用户。这就是产品主导型获客策略。我总结了几个核心类别。我认为我撰写的这篇文章之所以受欢迎，正是因为它提供了最优的创业增长路径。如果你的初创企业能通过产品主导型获客策略实现增长（并非所有企业都能做到，比如某些企业依赖销售团队），那么这无疑是最佳增长策略，因为用户邀请新用户的边际成本为零。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: It's scalable. It creates network graphs typically and has compounding effects there in terms of both moats and the ability to acquire more customers quickly. Basically to the point I just mentioned is basically viral. The other interesting thing here is there are far fewer dependencies. Let's say your company primarily grows via content and SEO, where you're at the mercy of Google releasing an algorithmic update let's say twice a year, which occasionally will absolutely tank your traffic and most people know what I mean by that if they've experienced that. It's awful.
turns.zh: 这种策略具有可扩展性，通常会形成网络效应，并在护城河构建和快速获取客户方面产生复合效应。正如我刚才提到的，其本质是病毒式传播。另外，这种策略的依赖性更低。以内容和SEO为主的增长策略为例，你必须依赖谷歌每年两次的算法更新——这些更新有时会导致流量骤降，相信有过类似经历的人都深有体会，这实在令人头疼。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Or ff you're a paid acquisition-led company, as opposed to a content-led acquisition company, meaning you're running Facebook Ads, let's just stick a Facebook for now, Facebook and Instagram, you're also at the mercy of the volatility of CPMs and whatever weird updates Facebook introduces or whatever targeting options they suddenly remove. Your entire acquisition strategy is anchored on something that is completely out of your hands and very volatile. Product-led acquisition is like the better you craft your product and the incentive structures for existing users inviting other users, that's entirely in your control and the better you grow.
turns.zh: 相反，如果你是一家以付费获客为主的公司（而非内容获客型公司），比如投放Facebook广告（暂且以Facebook为例，包括Facebook和Instagram），那么你同样受制于CPM波动、Facebook频繁更改广告投放规则或突然移除某些定向选项等不确定因素。你的整个获客策略完全依赖于超出你控制范围且极易波动的因素。而产品主导型获客策略则不同——你能精心设计产品，建立现有用户邀请新用户的激励机制，这完全在你的掌控之中，从而实现更优的增长。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: That's the quick context. Now, I'll go into some examples. We started with the example of... Actually one thing that came to mind that I love is Paul Graham, who we mentioned earlier, Paul Graham from YC, has this quote which is "don't start a startup where you need to go through someone else to get users." That always really resonated with me. Here are the categories of product-led acquisition that I've identified. Number one, like I mentioned, is users inviting other users to settle debts.
turns.zh: 以上就是简要背景。现在，我来举几个例子。我们先从一个例子说起……其实让我印象深刻的是保罗·格雷厄姆（Paul Graham），我们之前提到过，他来自YC公司。他曾说过：“如果你需要通过他人才能获得用户，那就别去创办初创公司。” 这句话一直让我深有共鸣。以下是我总结的几种产品驱动型获客模式。第一种，正如我之前提到的，是用户邀请其他用户来解决债务问题。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: If I'm going to pay you money I owe you for splitting dinner on Venmo, or a business expense that I'm paying you, you're my vendor on PayPal, or anything that's allowing me to just pay you money I owe you and I have to use a product to do so, whoever is collecting the money from me is going to make an account on that product if necessary to claim their hard earned money. Almost guaranteed way for you to have user-led growth, product-led growth. Now, it doesn't have to be money. It can be settling a debt of like an NFT, for example.
turns.zh: 比如，如果我要用Venmo向你支付晚餐分摊款，或者支付你的商业费用，你就是PayPal上的供应商。任何需要我通过产品来支付欠款的场景，收款方都必须在该产品上注册账户才能领取应得款项。这几乎是确保用户主导增长、产品驱动增长的必经之路。不过，不一定非得是金钱。例如，处理NFT交易的债务结算也可以采用类似方式。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Someone buys an NFT from you on OpenSea and the only way for them to receive their NFT, I'm just making this up right now, is to also have an OpenSea account or a wallet that's specific to that collection. Again, making this up. The point is if you're settling the debt of something you owe someone and they must make an account to capture the thing owed, they're going to sign up. That's category one. Category two is when you're inviting someone to join the product you're using to partake in a conversation that the otherwise cannot access. Why does Telegram, WhatsApp, iMessage, all these chat apps, Discord, grow so quickly?
turns.zh: 假设有人在OpenSea上从你那里购买NFT，而获取NFT的唯一途径（我现在只是假设）是注册OpenSea账户或创建特定于该收藏的钱包。关键在于，如果你需要通过产品来解决欠款问题，而对方必须注册账户才能领取欠款，他们就会注册。这就是第一种模式。第二种模式是邀请他人加入你正在使用的产品，参与他们原本无法访问的对话。为什么Telegram、WhatsApp、iMessage等聊天应用能如此迅速地增长？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Pretty obviously because if you and your little clique of friends are having your conversation in that app, then the person who's also in your real life friend group, but who hasn't yet installed the app has to install the app in order to have the conversation with you. Inviting people to critical, social, or business conversations in an app is the other way that you can nearly guarantee you'll grow very quickly from product-led acquisition. The business version of this is Slack. You sign up for Slack. You invite all your friends or all your coworkers. Then you even invite all your vendors via Slack Connect.
turns.zh: 原因很明显。如果你和你的小伙伴们在该应用中聊天，而你现实生活中的朋友还没安装该应用，就必须下载该应用才能与你对话。在应用中邀请他人参与关键社交或商务对话，是确保产品驱动型获客快速增长的另一种方式。Slack就是这种模式的商业化版本。你注册Slack，邀请所有朋友或同事，甚至通过Slack Connect邀请所有供应商。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Slack Connect was a brilliant Slack feature where they're saying, "Hey, we're now going to encourage you to invite people who aren't using Slack who are outside of your work." I don't know how that's done for them as a feature, but in theory, it's a brilliant way to expand the surface area for inviting people via product-led acquisition. Just to recap where we are real quick, one of the ways of acquiring customers is to encourage existing users, to pay other people or to encourage them to come into your app to have conversation that's only happening on the app.
turns.zh: Slack Connect是一个很棒的功能，他们通过这个功能鼓励用户邀请不在公司工作却与你有业务往来的人。虽然我不知道他们的具体实现方式，但从理论上讲，这是通过产品驱动型获客来扩大邀请用户范围的绝佳方式。最后快速回顾一下我们的主要观点：获取客户的一种方法是鼓励现有用户，通过支付他人、邀请他人加入应用等方式，让他们参与仅在应用内进行的对话。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: If I'm a product person and I'm road mapping my product, I will think, is there anything in my product conducive to either one of those two functionalities, settling debts, or can I introduce chat within my product? And if so, you might be cracking open an amazing channel. When I tell people about product-led acquisition, I'm usually doing it in the context of let's rethink your product feature roadmap to prioritize features that facilitate these things that can lead to explosive growth. I'll pause if there's anything you want to dive in there, but I have three more categories we could chat about if you want to, three more ways of doing PLA.
turns.zh: 假如我是一名产品经理，正在规划产品路线图，我会思考：我的产品中是否有功能能助力实现这两项功能——解决债务纠纷，或者能在产品中引入聊天功能？如果能做到这一点，你或许就能开辟一条惊人的增长渠道。当我向人们介绍产品主导型获客策略时，我通常会从重新审视产品功能路线图的角度出发，优先考虑那些能促进爆炸式增长的功能。如果你有任何想深入探讨的地方，我可以暂停一下，但如果方便的话，我们还有三个关于产品主导型获客策略的讨论方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I just want to lob a question over there as you're going through these to maybe touch on this. Most founders would love to find a way to grow through virality and invites and all the things you're talking about. I find that it's often hard to lop onto something they're doing, if it's not a natural fit. As you're going through this, I'd love to know how often have you seen startups succeed adding something like this when their app is not a money exchange app or a chat app? I'm curious how often it works to add something like this when your app's kind of something else, if that makes sense?
turns.zh: 是的，当然。我只是想在你讲解这些内容时，顺便提一个问题，也许能稍微拓展一下思路。大多数创始人都希望通过病毒式传播、邀请机制以及你提到的所有策略来实现增长。但如果这些策略与现有产品不契合，往往很难强行嫁接到现有产品中。在你分析过程中，想了解一下，在应用并非资金交易平台或聊天应用的情况下，添加这类功能成功的案例多吗？我很好奇，当应用本质是其他类型时，添加这类功能的成功率有多高？如果这能说得通的话。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Well, the real lesson is don't start a company if you have no idea how it's going to grow. Now, that's not categorically true for all startups. It's irrelevant for deep tech and biotech and climate tech and all that stuff, but for a lot of these people starting SaaS companies where they intend to grow very quickly among B2B customers or B2C. The real point of what I'm saying is if you have three ideas before you as a founder and one of them lends itself to product-led acquisition really beautifully, then lean in that direction perhaps if you think that growth is the key differentiator between them for what's going to lead to success.
turns.zh: 关键在于，如果作为创始人，你对产品如何增长毫无头绪，那就别轻易创办公司。当然，这并非适用于所有初创企业。对于深科技、生物科技、气候科技等领域而言，这无关紧要。但对于许多希望在B2B客户或B2C市场中快速增长的SaaS公司而言，关键在于：如果你作为创始人有三个创意方向，其中一个能完美适配产品主导型获客策略，那么就应该朝着这个方向倾斜——如果增长是区分成功与失败的关键因素的话。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: It's like make life easier on yourself. Because if we're relying so heavily on SEO and content, which is extremely saturated, or paid acquisition, meaning ad channels which are extremely saturated, especially if you have low LTVs where we can't really tolerate the volatility of paid CAC or just the cost in general of those CACs, then we have to be thinking more strategically at the product level. It's less about tacking it on later, but sometimes this will work brilliantly if it's very organic. When we cover my next category, we'll actually see some examples of how you can pack it on more seamlessly.
turns.zh: 这就像是给自己减轻负担。因为如果我们过度依赖SEO和内容（这个领域已高度饱和）或付费获客（即广告渠道，也已高度饱和），特别是当用户生命周期价值低、无法承受付费获客的波动性或其成本过高时，我们就必须在产品层面进行更具战略性的思考。这不是事后拼凑，而是有时候如果能自然融合，这种策略会效果极佳。在探讨下一类别时，我们将看到更多更无缝融合的案例。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: But the other response to your question, which is a great question, is people mistake product-led acquisition for referral programs, which it is not. Because the referral programs are a tact on incentive trying to give people something to encourage them to invite because they otherwise are not inviting. Whereas PLA, as I've currently defined it, is through the natural use of the product, you get more value when you invite others. You settle your debt with the payment recipient. You get have a better conversation because now your friend Jack is part of the conversation. You don't have to incentivize them with anything artificial, with any rewards.
turns.zh: 但对于你的问题（这是一个很棒的问题），我的另一个回应是，人们常把产品主导型获客策略误认为是推荐计划，但其实两者不同。推荐计划是通过激励手段，试图通过奖励来鼓励用户邀请他人，但产品主导型获客策略正如我目前所定义的，是通过产品的自然使用，让用户在邀请他人时获得更多价值。用户与支付方解决债务纠纷。用户能进行更好的对话，因为现在你的朋友杰克也加入了对话。你无需用任何虚假的奖励来刺激他们。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Referral programs generally are not exciting to me because you're usually trying to... Again, you're like self-selecting for folks who just want the reward very often. And then the people they invite might also just want the dual ended reward and they're not even here for the app really. And then they can bounce. And then they don't invite other people typicall.y. It doesn't have the same compounding sticky retentive nature of PLA. I'm not a fan of it. If you can make a work though, fantastic. Anyway, third category is what I call billboarding. Billboarding is this idea that the use of the product is inherently visible to people around you.
turns.zh:
推荐计划通常对我来说没什么吸引力，因为参与者往往是自觉选择那些只想获得奖励的人。而被邀请的人可能也只是为了双赢的奖励，根本不关注应用本身，结果很快就会流失，也不太会主动邀请其他人。这种模式缺乏PLA（Product-Lifetime Value）所具备的复合粘性留存特质。我对此不太感冒。不过如果你能成功打造这样的模式，那当然很棒。  

第三类我称之为"广告牌效应"。这种策略的核心在于产品使用过程本身就能自然地向周围人展示品牌信息。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: The product advertises itself. A few examples. Actually, where I got the term from is I was looking at these billboards above the highway in San Francisco, where I was seeing the company that actually hosts the billboards advertise their own logo on the billboard while also showing you whatever ad they were being paid to show. They were using their own surface area to advertise themselves. Another example is when you're seeing an ad network across the web, like Google banner ads perhaps, and it says they're brought to you by Google Ads, they're using their own surface area to advertise themselves.
turns.zh: 比如，旧金山高速公路上方的广告牌。广告牌主会把自己的标志印在上面，同时展示合作品牌的广告，充分利用自身的展示面进行品牌宣传。再比如网页上的广告网络，比如谷歌横幅广告，显示"由Google Ads呈现"等信息，也是利用自身平台进行品牌推广。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: That's billboarding. It's a brilliant free way to get a ton more exposure. There's a few ways to do billboarding. One is the classic example of Hotmail and iPhone. When you send an email via Hotmail, at the end, it pens a signature saying sent via Hotmail. Same thing, sent from my iPhone. Every single email sent from an iPhone device, unless you remove that signature, is a free billboard for Apple itself, which further furthers the brand awareness and gets more people buying.
turns.zh:
这就是广告牌效应。这种免费的曝光方式堪称绝妙。实现广告牌效应有两种方式：  
1. 典型案例：Hotmail和iPhone。Hotmail发送的邮件末尾会显示"由Hotmail发送"，iPhone发送的邮件则标注"由iPhone发送"。这些信息都是免费的品牌宣传，有助于提升品牌知名度和用户转化率。  

2. 应用场景：当应用支持用户向外部发送邮件或消息时，比如SMS短信应用、供应商发票系统等，可以在邮件签名中加入品牌信息，充分利用自身平台进行品牌推广。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: For example, if you have a feature in your application where people are sending emails or communications to other users outside of the org, like it's an app for sending SMS messages or it's like a way to send invoices to your vendors, when you're facilitating that generated messaging, say brought to you by the name of your startup in the signature of it, really use your own surface area to increase your own awareness. That's billboarding in two different ways. The third way is the very obvious way of having something unmistakably recognizable out in the world.
turns.zh: 第三种方式是最直接的"可见性广告"。比如开特斯拉、穿耐克鞋、用苹果AirPods等，这些实体产品本身就是移动广告牌。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: If I drive a Tesla, if I wear Nike shoes, if I have Apple AirPods, all of these are immediately visible to everyone around me, which is why sometimes physical products can really explode because they're just free walking billboards all over the world. And then the sort of most topical hot example right now on Twitter is when you switch your Twitter profile to an NFT in a particular collection, you're billboarding for that NFT collection, right? Same phenomenon that occurred with the Bitcoin laser eyes.
turns.zh: 推特上的NFT头像展示也是广告牌效应的典型案例。用户将个人资料切换为特定NFT系列时，相当于为该NFT系列做宣传，引发了广泛关注。比特币激光眼镜的案例同样说明了这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also for Twitter Blue, to be able to even do that.
turns.zh: 推特Blue功能也支持这种策略。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Yes, exactly. Exactly right. Like Telegram right now, they released something like Twitter Blue. I forget, I don't know what it's called. But now when you're a Telegram premium paying user, it has a little star thing next to your name that everyone else sees. "Wait, what is that? Oh, that's Telegram Pro. Let me take a look at that." Last example, which is one of my favorites, is billboarding via the nature of your product being something people are compelled to share in order to use. If I have a Calendly account, I have to share my Calendly link with the world in order to create an event on my calendar.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。比如Telegram现在推出了类似Twitter Blue的付费会员服务。我记不清具体叫什么名字了，但现在如果你是Telegram的付费用户，你的名字旁边会出现一个小星星标识，所有人都能看到。“等等，这是什么？哦，原来是Telegram Pro啊，让我看看。”最后一个例子，也是我最喜欢的案例之一，就是通过产品本身的特性实现口碑传播。例如，如果我有Calendly账户，就必须把我的Calendly链接分享给全世界，才能在日历上创建活动。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: If you're like me, you get a million Calendly links every week. That's the phenomenal form of billboarding, people are sharing it willingly. No wonder they've exploded. Same thing with Dropbox sharing file links and you're seeing the Dropbox URL, or GoFundMe, when people share the GoFundMe page. You get the gist. Billboarding costs you nothing, scales infinitely, can have compounding effects. And if your product lends itself to billboarding, it's just a phenomenal way to grow if possible. That's category three, I guess. We'll cover one last one, if you'd like me too, which is basically UGC, so user generated content.
turns.zh: 如果你和我一样，每周都会收到无数Calendly链接。这就是口碑传播的神奇之处——人们会主动分享。难怪这些产品能迅速走红。Dropbox分享文件链接也是如此，当人们分享GoFundMe页面时，你会看到GoFundMe的网址。总之，你懂的。口碑传播成本极低，规模无限，效果往往能叠加。如果你的产品本身适合口碑传播，那这无疑是一种极佳的增长策略。这应该属于第三类策略。最后再讲一个例子，用户生成内容（UGC）。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Same sort of thing. Basically I hop on YouTube or TikTok or Insta or whatever. I make content. I share it with the world. In so sharing that content, the platforms brand themselves on the content. At the end of every TikTok video on Twitter that you've ever seen or Insta, at the end it'll say, "Here's the TikTok user's account." They're billboarding themselves into the content that users themselves are generating, and the users are incentivized to share that content off platform, which brings users to the platform, because users want to get customers wherever they can. They're going to cross-sell to their YouTube channel and so on.
turns.zh: 道理类似。比如我在YouTube、TikTok、Instagram或其他平台上创作内容并分享。通过这种分享，平台会将自身品牌植入到内容中。你是否注意到TikTok视频在Twitter或Instagram上的结尾都会显示“这是TikTok用户的账号”。他们把自己的品牌植入到用户生成的内容中，而用户也被激励将这些内容分享到其他平台，从而为平台带来新用户，因为用户总想尽可能多地获取客户。他们还会交叉推广到自己的YouTube频道等平台。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: If you have a marketplace like eBay or some marketplace for selling collectible shoes or something where you're encouraging users to create beautiful content of the items being sold, like these cool landing pages that show off the products, and they share it elsewhere, then that's an example of users making content they're sharing off platform that is useful for their own followers. Another example of UGC that people often overlook is Quora or Reddit or Stack Overflow or TripAdvisor, where you're encouraging users to create content in the form of conversation that then surface itself on Google and SEO.
turns.zh: 如果你运营eBay之类的市场平台，或者销售收藏鞋类等商品的市场平台，鼓励用户为所售商品创作精美的内容，比如那些展示产品的酷炫登陆页面，然后用户将这些内容分享到其他平台，这就是用户创造有用内容并在平台外分享的例子。UGC中常被忽视的例子还有Quora、Reddit、Stack Overflow或TripAdvisor等平台，你鼓励用户以对话形式创作内容，而这些内容会出现在Google搜索结果中并提升SEO效果。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Basically if you just encourage users to have conversations that are publicly indexed, that increases your surface area on Google for hitting more keywords and you get way more search traffic. Basically the question that this boils down to is to leverage UGC in your product, you ask yourself, do users use my product to make content in any way, shape, or form? If so, what type of content that they make should we encourage them to then share? And then how can we make the page that they use to share the content as appealing and as easily to consume as possible? And that's basically UGC. We'll pause there, but basically that's PLA in a nutshell.
turns.zh: 基本上，如果你鼓励用户公开创作内容，就能增加Google搜索关键词的曝光量，从而获得更多搜索流量。归根结底，利用UGC策略需要思考两个问题：用户是否以任何形式使用你的产品来创作内容？如果是，那我们应该鼓励他们分享哪种类型的内容？然后，如何让他们分享内容的页面尽可能吸引人且易于消费？这就是UGC的精髓。我们先到这里，总之，PLA（Product-led Acquisition）策略的核心要义就是如此。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: The thing that all of these have in common is you're not spending a dollar. They scale super quickly. You're not reliant on, well, maybe to some extent with SEO, but you're not relying on third party volatility. It's a much healthier narrative for how you're going to grow and scale.
turns.zh: 这些方法的共同点是无需花费一分钱。它们扩展得极为迅速。你无需依赖第三方平台的波动性（虽然在SEO方面可能需要一定程度的依赖）。这为你的业务增长和扩展提供了更为健康的发展路径。
