turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We talked about acquisition, which we'll link to in the show notes, by the way, this whole post. The flip side you could say is retention. If you're a reader of my newsletter, you know how much time I spend thinking about retention and how important that is. I know that's a second topic that we wanted to chat about, because you've also helped a lot of companies think through their retention strategies and to help them retain more users. I'm curious to hear what you've found to be the best strategies for retaining users and increasing retention.
turns.zh: 我们讨论了用户获取（顺便说一下，我们会在节目笔记中附上相关链接），反面来说就是用户留存。如果你是我的新闻通讯读者，你就知道我花了多少时间思考用户留存问题，以及它有多么重要。我知道这是我们想聊的第二个话题，因为你也帮助过许多公司思考他们的用户留存策略，帮助他们留住更多用户。我很想听听你认为留住用户和提高用户留存率的最佳策略是什么。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Yeah, sure. The way I think about retention, my favorite strategy is what I call building state. It's a concept I stole from video games, where basically the more you play any given game, the more state you're accruing. That might be your armor, your weapons, your character skins, and whatever. As a player of the game, the more state you build, the more you're compelled to stick around, because you don't want to lose everything you've worked so hard for. The more state you have, the more you can exploit that state to get more. The rich keep getting richer. The same mental models apply to let's say SaaS retention.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。我思考用户留存的方式，我最喜欢的策略是所谓的“建立状态”。这个概念是我从电子游戏中借鉴来的，基本上你玩任何一款游戏越多，积累的状态就越多。这些可能包括你的盔甲、武器、角色皮肤等等。作为游戏玩家，积累的状态越多，你就越有动力继续留在游戏中，因为你不想失去自己努力得来的一切。积累的状态越多，你就越能利用这些状态来获得更多利益。富人会越来越富。同样的思维模式也适用于SaaS领域的用户留存问题。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: This is as old as time, or at least as old as modern capitalism. If you think of credit card rewards or frequent flyer programs, you spend money. You accrue points. You convert the points into rewards. Once users build momentum doing that, they're less likely to switch to a competitor. That's the age old example of building state. Software, it's unbelievably powerful. This building state concept is why mediocre companies like eBay or Craigslist remain completely unbeatable for decades. Even though the UX is bad, people don't like using them, they fail to innovate, no one topples them and it's because of state.
turns.zh: 这是古老而永恒的商业智慧，或者至少是现代资本主义的永恒法则。想想信用卡奖励积分或飞行常客计划，你花钱消费，积累积分，再将积分兑换成奖励。一旦用户形成这种习惯，他们就更不愿意转投竞争对手。这就是建立用户粘性的经典案例。软件的魔力令人惊叹。正是这种建立用户粘性的理念，让eBay、Craigslist等平庸公司数十年来始终牢不可破。尽管用户体验糟糕、产品缺乏创新，但用户始终无法撼动它们的地位，这一切都源于用户粘性。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Let's walk through some examples. State, kind of like my PLA mega spiel, mega rant there, subdivides into a few categories, but I'll make this one shorter and less boring. The first subcategory of building state is when you're encouraging your users to accrue non-transferrable reputation, meaning they're doing stuff to build reputation on the platform and they cannot take that reputation to them off platform. They're stuck there to get the compounding advantage of that reputation. For example, let's say you've spent years getting 10,000 or more feedback ratings as an eBay seller.
turns.zh: 让我们举几个例子。用户粘性（就像我之前在PLA上的长篇大论）可以分为几个子类别，但这次我会简化并减少枯燥内容。第一个子类别是鼓励用户积累不可转移的声誉，即用户在平台上积累声誉，但无法将其转移到其他平台。用户被锁定在平台上，只能享受声誉带来的复合效益。例如，假设你作为eBay卖家，花费数年时间积累了1万条或更多反馈评分。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: You are not leaving eBay anytime soon, because that reputation's just too valuable. It's producing a huge boost in revenue because of the trust it engenders with buyers on eBay. It probably results in you ranking better in search results for an eBay query. Because you cannot move those 10,000 feedbacks to an eBay competitor, you're not incentivized to go use an eBay competitor. This type of stickiness, this non-transferrable reputation, basically applies to all marketplaces and directories. Same thing on Yelp. You as a restaurant build your reputation on Yelp. The momentum keeps you stuck there. You want to keep getting reviews and hone your reviews.
turns.zh: 你短期内不会离开eBay，因为这些声誉太有价值了。它为eBay买家带来信任，显著提升了你的收入，可能让你在eBay搜索结果中排名更高。由于这些1万条反馈无法转移到eBay竞争对手那里，你就没有动力转投其他平台。这种用户粘性（不可转移的声誉）适用于所有市场和目录平台。Yelp也是如此。作为餐厅，你在Yelp上积累声誉，形成的势头让你难以离开。用户希望不断获得评价并提升评价质量。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Airbnb with your properties, Etsy, for you as a seller, Alibaba, all of this stuff are examples of companies that are kind of old now, cannot be top old or haven't been yet. People are like, why? Well, because of this exact reason. This is why those companies pester you so much to leave reviews and provide feedback all the time. They want you to play into this game of in market reputation building. The second state building technique that a startup could adopt, and again, this is all under the guise of how do we maximize retention and build somewhat of a moat, for example, the second way you can do this is you encourage your users to accrue a non-transferable audience.
turns.zh: Airbnb的房产、Etsy的卖家、阿里巴巴等，这些如今已成巨头或即将成为巨头的公司，都在采用这种策略。人们不禁问：为什么？原因就在于此。这就是为什么这些公司不断催促你写评价、提供反馈，试图让你陷入平台声誉积累的循环。第二种建立用户粘性的策略，也是以提升用户留存率和构建护城河为目标。例如，你可以鼓励用户积累不可转移的受众群体。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: If I'm a big YouTuber and I've acquired a million subs, those subs can't be transferred anywhere else. I can't bring them to Twitter. In fact, YouTube doesn't even tell me their email, so I can't even bring them to a newsletter if I wanted to. The more subs you acquire on YouTube, the easier it is for you to go viral on YouTube. This is what I mean earlier by the rich keep getting richer. It's this momentum trap. It's very, very hard to convince any YouTuber to get off YouTube. If anything, they'll dabble with another network in parallel at best.
turns.zh: 如果我是YouTube大主播，积累了百万订阅用户，这些订阅无法转移到其他平台。我甚至无法获取他们的邮箱地址，如果我想将他们导入通讯列表也无从下手。YouTube上订阅用户越多，内容在平台上爆红的机会就越大。这就是我之前说的"富者恒富"的含义。这是一个势头陷阱。说服YouTuber离开YouTube极其困难。即便如此，他们最多也就是在其他平台上尝试合作，但效果往往不尽如人意。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Basically if you have a startup where you're creating a marketplace or an audience graph, you want to encourage users to build a follower graph within that product that they can take advantage of by pushing their product or their content or their insights too. This is why Twitter... By the way, a big shout out to Substack, which actually allows customers to export emails off of Substack. Substack is not playing that same game, which is better for users and a very nice thing for the ecosystem. But this is why Twitch and Instagram and Twitter are just irreplaceable. I mean, not necessarily. Everything dies over time like Facebook, but they're just so darn hard to topple.
turns.zh: 基本上，如果你经营一家初创公司，正在打造一个市场平台或用户图谱，就需要鼓励用户在该产品中建立自己的粉丝图谱。用户可以利用这些数据推广自己的产品、内容或见解。这就是Twitter如此不可替代的原因。不过话说回来，Substack确实值得称赞，它允许用户将邮件数据导出。这家公司没有采用那种用户数据封闭的策略，这对用户和整个生态系统来说都是件好事。但这也恰恰说明了Twitch、Instagram和Twitter为何难以被取代。当然，也不一定非得如此。Facebook之类的平台终将衰落，但这些巨头实在太难撼动了。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Let's maybe touch one more. I don't want to ramble so much about this. Well, this one's kind of similar. Basically if you spent a lot of time building a social graph in a product, like if I spent the last 10 years trying to remember the names of all my high school friends and elementary school friends and add them one at a time over the years to Facebook, or I've added all my colleagues for the last 20 years onto LinkedIn and I've built a social graph on these products where I've curated and found people, that's really sticky. You're building state in the form of taking time to expand the graph. The graph is a representative of the state, the work you've put in.
turns.zh: 再举个例子。我不想在这方面说得太冗长。不过这个例子和前一个类似。假设你花了大量时间在产品中构建社交图谱——比如说，我过去十年一直试图记住高中和小学同学的名字，一年又一年地把他们添加到Facebook上，或者过去20年把同事都加到LinkedIn上，在这些产品中建立社交图谱、筛选并找到朋友，这就是高度粘性的做法。你在扩展图谱上投入了大量精力，而图谱本身就是你所付出的努力的象征。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: You don't want to lose those connections with people. That makes that product extra sticky. This is why social networks in general can be sticky. It's not just the fact that you have your audience there, it's that you've invested time. If Facebook doesn't allow you to export your graph out, then that makes it extra sticky as well, because you don't know how else to talk to old Jimmy from elementary other than Facebook. Anyway, there's actually many more of these examples of building state. I'm going to just stop with that. But the basic concept is what can you encourage users to do within your product that makes them more deeper entrenched in the product, and most apps just completely lack this.
turns.zh: 你肯定不想失去和这些人的联系。这会让产品更加难以割舍。这就是社交网络普遍具有粘性的原因。关键不在于用户群体在那里，而在于你投入了时间。如果Facebook不允许导出用户图谱，那就更难割舍了，因为除了Facebook，你根本找不到和小学同学Jimmy联系的其他方式。总之，构建用户粘性的例子还有很多。我就说到这儿。但核心概念是，你要鼓励用户在产品中做些什么，让他们更深入地融入产品，而大多数应用在这方面都做得很差。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. It's a little bit like the concept of having skin in the game and just building more skin in the game with the product that you're using. One quick question, is there a company that you've seen do this, like add it on, and succeed and increased retention that you've worked with or out there? Just like is there a good example that comes to mind that added this piece?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个概念。这有点像“亲身参与其中，全身心投入”的理念。快速问一下，你有没有见过哪个公司这样做并成功提升用户留存率的？有没有什么好的例子？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Again, none of this is really under the context of telling people to add it on after they've decided what they're building. This is all in the DNA of the product you're choosing to build. I'm not sure. I haven't thought of those examples. I'm thinking more so in whose DNA, which company's DNA are they doing this brilliantly? For example, one form of state is... One I did not cover is when you're embedded infrastructure. If you're Twilio, Striper, AWS, it's really hard to move off or segment because it's so much work to redo your code and introduce all this risk to screwing up your code base. People have built patterns around how they work with your API.
turns.zh: 再说一次，这些都不是在告诉人们产品上线后再添加这些功能。这应该深深植根于你选择打造的产品的DNA中。我不确定。我还没想到这样的例子。我更想知道的是，在哪些公司的DNA中，他们把这项工作做得特别出色？比如说，用户依赖的某项基础设施。如果你用的是Twilio、Stripe、AWS之类的服务，想要迁移或分割出去实在太困难了，因为重写代码并引入所有风险会让代码库崩溃。人们围绕如何使用你的API已经形成了固定的模式。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: A lot of modern API startups automatically capture the stickiness by virtue of being so deeply embedded into a product. Generally speaking, none of this is in the context of like, hey, add it on post hoc, pretty much.
turns.zh: 很多现代API初创公司通过深度嵌入产品，自动捕捉用户粘性。总的来说，这些都不是事后添加功能的范畴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. I like that lens actually through a lot of these things you're talking about is maybe it's less like change your product to make this happen, and it's more idea selection. I know you're also an investor, and so it's a really good lens on how many of these things does this company have that I'm investing in.
turns.zh: 明白了。实际上，我很欣赏你提到的这个视角——虽然你提到的很多东西可能需要调整产品来实现，但本质上是选题筛选。我知道你也是一位投资者，所以这确实能很好地让我了解我所投资的公司在这些方面有何布局。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Earlier I was mentioning why do I write handbooks, I wrote the handbook that PLA and state building come from to cement my diligence criteria for companies I believe might grow super fast and retain customers. You're exactly right. My investor's perspective is if you have a zero cost of acquisition mechanism for customer acquisition, such as PLA, and you can retain them through something like state building, but there are other ways to retain customers, then I lean in harder because I think you'll be more defensible as a company. Actually interesting little side note is you'll often hear retention and stickiness refer to as a moat, right?
turns.zh: 之前我提到过为什么我要写手册，比如我写了关于PLA和State Building的分析手册，就是为了固化我对可能实现超快速增长并留住客户的公司的尽职调查标准。你说得很对。从投资者的角度来看，如果一家公司有零成本获取客户的机制，比如PLA，同时能通过State Building等手段留住客户——当然还有其他留存客户的途径——那我会更倾向于深入研究，因为我认为这样能增强公司的护城河效应。一个有趣的小插曲是，你经常听到人们把留存和用户粘性称为护城河，对吧？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: But I find this term actually very misleading because very few companies have actual moats. To have a real moat, you're basically exploiting kleptocratic, meaning you're friends with the government and they're creating a literal barrier to entry for your competitors, or you have a scientific moat where you have an actual scientific breakthrough in the fusion energy space, plus protected by patents. Those are real moats. But the way most people use the word moat is wrong. In practice, your "moat" is just your mechanism for retaining users a little bit more than the average company.
turns.zh: 但我觉得这个术语其实很误导人，因为很少有公司真正拥有护城河。要真正拥有护城河，你要么是利用裙带关系，比如与政府关系密切，政府为竞争对手设置进入壁垒；要么是在聚变能领域实现科学突破并获得专利保护。这些才是真正的护城河。但大多数人对护城河的理解是错误的。实际上，所谓的“护城河”不过是留住用户的机制，仅此而已。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I believe state building is one of the best ways to do exactly that. Really it just comes down to what are you doing to help users build state and get more value over time out of the product, not the same level of value over any time period.
turns.zh: 我认为State Building就是实现这一目标的最佳方式之一。关键在于，你要做些什么来帮助用户逐步建立状态，并从产品中获得更多长期价值，而非短暂的即时满足。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Shifting a little bit away from growth and into writing, which I know you've spent a lot of time writing about, very meta, and sharing on Twitter and all the ways, you have a handbook where you go into this concept of novelty and a framework for how to be novel and why that's important in writing. I'd love for you to talk about why novelty is important in writing and ideally share your framework for creating something novel that keeps people engaged in reading.
turns.zh: 太棒了。稍微转向写作领域——我知道你花了很多时间研究写作，非常有自觉性，还在推特上分享心得——你有一本手册，探讨了新奇性的概念，并提供了如何创新以及创新为何对写作至关重要的框架。我很想听听你为什么认为新奇性对写作很重要，最好能分享一下你创建新奇内容、吸引读者兴趣的框架。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Sure. This actually goes back to your question about Twitter. What can one do to build an audience on Twitter? It often comes down to writing things that are novel. Novel is what powers click bait in most cases. The other way is via curiosity gap, where you raise a question you don't answer, but the other half is novelty is what gets people to click into a thread and read it. Novelty, I define, as new idea, so something I haven't heard of before, that's also significant, so it's not some trivial fact about Kim Kardashian, and it's something that I wouldn't have easily intuited on my own.
turns.zh: 当然。这其实回到了你之前关于推特的问题。如何在推特上建立受众？关键在于写出新奇的内容。新奇性往往是大多数点击诱饵的核心。另一种方法是利用好奇心缺口，即提出一个未解答的问题，但其中一半内容是新奇的，能吸引人们点击进入话题并阅读。对我来说，新奇性意味着新想法——即我从未听说过的、且具有重大意义的内容——而不是关于金·卡戴珊的琐碎趣闻，也不是我自己轻易能想到的东西。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: When you have those ingredients, it's new, it's significant, and you wouldn't have easily thought of it on your own, that's when you trigger that dopamine hit reaction, I'm not being scientifically accurate here, but you're going to get that dopamine hit like, "Whoa! That's super cool." The more you have readers pausing going, "Whoa! That was interesting," the more novel your writing is. My whole approach to writing is write something out, and then point out all the points of novelty. I do that by actually having 20 friends read something I've written and highlight the sentences that made them go, "Whoa."
turns.zh: 只要具备了这些要素，内容就会变得新颖且引人注目，读者很可能难以自行想到这样的创意——这正是能激发多巴胺奖赏反应的关键所在。我这里说得不够科学，但你肯定会感受到那种惊喜感：“哇！太酷了！” 当越来越多的读者停下来感叹“哇！真有趣！” 时，你的作品就越具创新性。我写作的整个思路就是先写出初稿，然后找出所有具有新意的点。我会让20位朋友通读我的文章，标出那些让他们惊叹“哇！”的句子。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: And then I have this visualized map in a given blog post, where are the areas that people go, "That's really interesting," and then I can see all the white space between the interesting parts. I go in and I condense that white space. I chop it down so that the frequency of novelties as high as possible. This is how you get a blog post that just has this phenomenal momentum that gets the read to completion rate to be very high. The question is, what exactly does novelty look like? I've identified about five different categories for it, and this is the backbone of how I write in many cases.
turns.zh: 之后，我会在博客文章中 visualize 出读者停留的区域，标出那些让他们说“真有趣”的地方。这样我就能看到有趣段落之间的空白区域，进而进行精简，尽可能提高新意的密度。这样才能写出一篇拥有惊人势头的博文，让读完率大增。问题是，新意到底该如何呈现？我总结了五大类新意模式，这也是我写作的核心理念。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: The first category of novelty is what I call counterintuitive information. You tell people something and they go, "Oh wow. I never realized that the world worked that way," or different categories and you tell people counter-narrative information. That's where people respond, "Wow. That's not how I was told the world worked." Whereas counterintuitive novelty is, "That's not how I would've thought the world worked," counter-narrative novelty is, "That's not what I've been told. I've been lied to. Now you're telling me the truth." That also triggers a dopamine hit. Third category of novelty is just pure shock and awe like, "That's crazy. I would've never believed that's true."
turns.zh: 第一类新意我称之为反直觉信息。你告诉读者某个事实，他们会惊呼：“哇，原来世界是这样运作的！”第二类是反叙事信息。比如当你指出与他们所知相反的观点时，他们会回应：“哇，原来世界不是这样的。” 而反直觉新意则是“我从未想过世界会这样运作”，反叙事新意则是“我被误导了，现在你告诉我真相了。” 这同样能激发多巴胺奖赏反应。第三类新意是纯粹的震惊与惊叹，比如“太不可思议了。我绝不会相信这是真的。”

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: For example, there's a volcano that's going to erupt the next 15 years that's going to swallow this whole island. Wow, that's shocking. Holy moly. Next category is what a lot of popular Twitter users do is what I call elegant articulation, where you're taking an idea... Naval does this, Naval on Twitter, the founder of AngelList. He'll say something that's a complicated rich thought and boil it down into a very concise sentence. And then the reader goes, "Wow, that's beautiful. I couldn't have said that any better myself."
turns.zh: 例如，未来15年内将爆发的火山会吞没整个岛屿。哇，太震惊了。第四类是许多热门推特用户常用的技巧，我称之为优雅表达。比如 Naval（AngelList创始人）会把复杂的思想浓缩成简洁的句子，读者会感叹：“哇，太妙了。我自己都想不出这么好的表达。”

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: That also triggers that dopamine reaction. There's a few more, but the point I want to get at here is all of these are formats for identifying the types of things you could say to get people to go, "Whoa." That's what I think of as novelty.
turns.zh: 这些都是激发读者惊叹的技巧，我认为这就是新意的本质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I've found to kind of identify something that I've written is going to be interesting is I just read it myself and I feel what I feel when I'm reading it the first time. Often I find that if I'm like, "Oh wow, this is really good and really exciting," I've learned to trust that feeling wherever that comes from. That's just like another way of knowing if your thing is interesting is like, are you excited about it? Are you interested in it as you're reading it? And that fades after you read it like 10 times and kind of edit and edit, but that's just a small tip I've learned, just kind of trust your own gut feeling when you're excited about something that you're writing about.
turns.zh: 我发现，要判断自己写的东西是否有趣，一个方法就是自己再读一遍，感受初读时的感受。通常，如果我会想“哇，真不错，太激动人心了”，说明这个想法值得信赖。判断一个点子是否有趣的另一个方法是，你读它时是否感到兴奋？你是否对它感兴趣？但当你读十遍、反复修改后，那种感觉可能就会消失。不过这只是我学到的一个小技巧——当你对自己正在写的内容感到兴奋时，就该相信自己的直觉了。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I agree. And that's why I tell people when you first encounter something that to you is novel, write down with a score, like let's say out a five, zero to five, how novel that thing was to you when you first heard it. You want to remember and capture the degree of novelty, because to your point, Lenny, it's going to become less novel over time. And then if you pull that out of your idea bank for a blog post in two years, it'll like, oh yeah, that will blow people's minds, even it doesn't blow my mind today.
turns.zh: 我同意。这就是为什么我告诉人们，当你第一次遇到新奇的事物时，先给它打个分，比如从0到5，评判它对你来说有多新奇。记住并捕捉这种新鲜感很重要，因为正如你所说，Lenny，随着时间推移，新奇感会逐渐消失。两年后当你从创意库中翻出这个点子用于博客时，人们会惊叹不已，即便现在它并不能让你惊艳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good tip.
turns.zh: 好建议。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: To your point, the way you basically get novel ideas is you go live your life and write down every time you come across something that interests or surprises you, or any time you come across something that makes you think, "Well, that's obviously not true," meaning you found something that people say that you know the lie and you're about to tell people the way the world really works. Some examples of novelty... I'm scrolling through Twitter up here. This is a tweet I wrote where I wrote, "Reading many books is the most socially accepted vanity metric for adults." I give zero kudos for reading a hundred books a year, but I give you massive kudos for learning efficiently and making interesting things.
turns.zh: 正如你所说，获取新奇想法的关键在于生活体验。每次遇到感兴趣或令人惊讶的事物，或者每次发现人们所说的谎言时，都记录下来。比如，当你发现人们常说某个观点是错的，而你正要去纠正他们时。这里有几个新奇的例子……我正在浏览推特。这是我写的一条推文：“阅读大量书籍是成年人最被社会认可的虚荣指标。”我对每年读100本书的人毫无敬意，但我非常赞赏那些高效学习并创造有趣事物的人。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: This tweet is an example of me using novelty. As we read the key novel part, it's where I say, "Reading many books is the most socially accepted vanity metric for adults." That is counter-narrative novelty, because the prevailing narrative is all the smart people I've ever met, they read a ton of books. They always have a book in their hand. They're reading five books a month, blah blah, blah, blah, blah. I'm saying no, that's a vanity metric how many books you read. That's counter-narrative. That gives people a dopamine hit. They lean in. They want to see what my punchline is and that tweet got a lot of engagement.
turns.zh: 这条推文就是我利用新奇元素的例子。关键的新奇点在于我说：“阅读大量书籍是成年人最被社会认可的虚荣指标。” 这属于反叙事型新奇，因为主流叙事是所有我见过的聪明人，他们都读很多书。他们手里总有一本书，每月读五本之类的。而我说不，这只是你读了多少书的虚荣指标。这就是反叙事，它能给人带来多巴胺冲击。他们会全神贯注，急切想知道我的妙语是什么，这条推文获得了大量互动。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: One more example. See if you can catch the novelty here. New tweet, "The world is not run by exceptional people. This is the hidden reason for imposter syndrome. We mistakenly think imposter syndrome is due to low confidence or low anxiety. No. It's caused by not accepting that your new world-class peers aren't that special. It's just discipline." The key statement there that has the novelty is the world is not run by exceptional people, and the type of novelty being used there is counterintuitive. Your intuition is the world's run by the best of the best or many of these experts are there for a reason.
turns.zh: 再举个例子。看看你能否捕捉到其中的新奇之处。这条新推文：“世界并非由杰出之人运转。这是冒名顶替综合症的隐藏原因。我们误以为冒名顶替综合症源于低自信或低焦虑。不。它是因为不接受你身边新晋的世界级同行其实也没那么特别。这只是纪律性的问题。” 关键的观点是“世界并非由杰出之人运转”，这里运用的就是反直觉的新奇。你的直觉可能是世界由最优秀的人或许多专家主导才得以运转。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I'm saying not in most cases. Anyway, those are some examples of novelty. Of course, these tweets took off largely due to that reason. People love having their eyes opened. They'll reflexively retweet you to agree with your worldview if they feel like you're finally speaking truth, the power, in some sense, if that makes sense.
turns.zh: 我是说，在大多数情况下并非如此。不管怎样，这些推文之所以能走红，很大程度上就是因为这个原因。人们喜欢开拓视野。如果他们觉得你终于说出了真相、权威之类的话，他们就会下意识地转发你的推文来认同你的世界观——某种意义上说，这就是力量所在，如果你能理解的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll link to those in the show notes. By the way, I love your reading your own tweets voice that you have.
turns.zh: 我们会在节目笔记中附上相关链接。顺便说一句，我很喜欢你读自己推文时的语气。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I'm adopting my... Who's the guy from Star Trek who's amazing, who reads the kids?
turns.zh: 我正在模仿……《星际迷航》里那个超棒、给孩子们读书的家伙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah, LeVar Burton. Reading Rainbow.
turns.zh: 哦对了，是莱弗·伯顿。他主持的《阅读彩虹》节目。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: There you go. That's my voice.
turns.zh: 就是这样。这就是我的语气。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Julian Shapiro, the new LeVar Burton. I know you have to run in not too long from now. We have two more topics. How about I set up both topics and then you kind of talk through as much as you want with each? That sound good?
turns.zh: 朱利安·夏皮罗，新莱弗·伯顿。我知道你很快就要走了。我们还有两个话题。要不我先把两个话题都列出来，然后你想说多少就说多少？这样行吗？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. The fourth topic we want to talk about is topic selection, how meta, essentially picking what to write about, and you have a bunch of great advice on what's worth writing about and the framework around that. And then the fifth idea is something you called it the Creativity Faucet, which is essentially how to get more creative. I will turn it over to you to share your thoughts on these topics.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们想讨论的第四个话题是选题，讲得再具体点，就是如何选择写作主题。你在如何筛选值得写作的主题以及相关框架方面有很多很棒的建议。第五个想法是你称之为“创意龙头”的，本质上是如何变得更有创造力。我把话题交给你，你来分享对这些话题的看法。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Sure, sure. My pleasure. The way I think about topic selection, meaning what is it you should write about for your blog posts, for your newsletter, Twitter, company blog, whatever, books, is you choose topics based on two factors, what would you actually be able to complete so you're not going to give a pathway through and what will actually be high quality. I have a framework for helping you figure out what that is. Basically I believe that your likelihood to follow through on something you start writing is a function of the objective you have with writing that piece and how strong your motivation is for seeing that objective to fruition.
turns.zh: 好的，好的。乐意之至。我对选题的思考方式是，什么样的主题适合写博客、通讯、推特、公司博客、书籍之类的，关键在于两个因素：一是能否真正完成写作，二是能否产出高质量内容。我有一个帮助你确定这两点的框架。基本上，写作的完成概率取决于你写作的目标以及达成目标的动力。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Here's what that looks like more specifically. Anytime that I write something, I'm first trying to identify what is my objective. Here's a few examples of objectives that I'll use before sitting down to write. Number one, I want to open people's eyes to prove the status quo wrong, or two, I want to articulate something that everyone's thinking about, but no one is saying. I want to cut through the noise. Another objective might be, I want to contribute original insights to my own research and experimentation. Hence, some of my handbooks. Another objective is just telling a suspenseful and emotional story that maybe imparts a lesson.
turns.zh: 具体来说是这样的。每次写作前，我首先会明确自己的目标。比如，我想让人们意识到现状是错误的；或者，我想把大家心里想但没说出口的话说出来；我想突破噪音；还有，我想为自己的研究和实验贡献原创见解，这也是我写手册的原因；再或者，就是讲一个悬念迭起、情感充沛的故事，或许还能传递一些启示。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: These are all clear cut objectives that give me a guidepost. I know that I'm done writing a piece if I can read the piece and say, "I've accomplished that particular objective," because people don't know when they're done writing, "Oh, I petered out here and this seems like a good place for an outro." With an objective, you know whether you should actually stop. But then the question is, how do you sustain the motivation to see through an objective? Again, an objective might be something like open people's eyes by proving the status quo wrong. To do all the work necessary to accomplish that, you need a motivation in my opinion.
turns.zh: 这些都是明确的目标，它们为我指明了方向。我知道，当我读完一篇文章并能说"我达到了这个特定目标"时，就意味着这篇文章写完了。因为人们往往不知道什么时候该停止写作，"哦，我在这里卡住了，这里似乎是个收尾的好地方。"但有了目标，你就能判断是否该停笔了。但问题是，如何保持完成目标的动力呢？比如说，目标可能是通过证明现状是错误的来让人们大开眼界。要达成这个目标，需要有足够的动力。我的观点是，动机很重要。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I'll pair one of those objectives that I've selected with a motivation. Some example motivations are, does writing this piece get something off my chest that I really badly need to get off? Or does it help me solve a nagging unsolved problem that I've been dealing with and this piece is way for me to explore and find the solution? Or is it like me obsessing over a topic that I want others to also geek out about? These are all powerful motivations that I pair with an objective to guarantee my follow through to get done writing the piece.
turns.zh: 我会将我选定的目标与某种动机相匹配。比如，写这篇文章是为了发泄胸中郁结的情绪？还是为了解决一个困扰已久的难题？又或者是想让别人也为某个话题而着迷？这些都是强大的动机，我会将它们与目标相结合，确保能坚持完成写作。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: By the way, everything I've mentioned in this entire chat with you, the novelty stuff, the topic selection, PLA, state building, everything we've covered, I have tons of examples on Julian.com. That's why I'm not trying to go through every single one.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我在这次聊天中提到的所有内容——创新点子、选题策略、PLA、状态构建等等，我在Julian.com上都有大量案例。这就是为什么我不打算一一详述。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and we'll link to all that.
turns.zh: 是的，我们会附上所有链接。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: The flip side I'll point out is that I think writing quality overall is... Again, these are all me being hand wavy and these are not rules. There's no right way to write, just like there's no right way to paint. These are just frameworks I've developed, that when I use them, I'm more frequently arriving at success as far as I define it. The thing I want to point out though is that very closely tied to everything I'm talking about is my framework or my equation for determining how good any piece of writing is, is novelty times resonance. Writing quality equals novelty times resonance.
turns.zh: 另一方面，我想说的是，总体写作质量……再说一次，这些都是我的个人见解，并非铁律。写作没有标准答案，就像绘画没有标准方法一样。这些只是我开发的框架，使用它们时，我更容易达成我所定义的成功。然而，我想指出的是，与我所谈论的一切紧密相连的是我的框架或公式，用于衡量一篇作品的质量——创新性乘以共鸣。写作质量等于创新性乘以共鸣。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Novelty is like we discussed, here are all these things that are giving you dopamine hits where I'm opening your eyes about how the world really works and shocking you and elegantly synthesizing things, times resonance and resonance means I can tell you the most novel thing on the planet. But if I don't wrap it in a way that resonates and really lifts off the page and into your mind and is something you remember, then it's fairly ineffective novelty. It's more like just trivia. It's bland, dry trivia. When you add resonance to the novelty, now it becomes a beautifully written piece. Resonance is a matter of including examples, analogies, metaphors, stories.
turns.zh: 创新性就像我们讨论的那样，这里有各种能让你获得多巴胺快感的元素，比如让我打开你的眼界，展示世界的真实运作方式，让你感到震惊，并优雅地综合各种观点。而共鸣意味着我可以告诉你世界上最具创新性的东西。但如果我不以一种能在人们脑海中引发共鸣、真正跳出纸面、进入你心智并被铭记的方式来包装它，那这种创新就相当无效了。它不过是琐事，是平淡无味的琐事。当你将创新性与共鸣相结合时，它就成为了一篇精心写作的作品。共鸣在于加入例子、类比、比喻和故事。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Really writing quality is novelty times the storytelling power you have to make the novelty resonate in the back of people's minds. The way that I structure my writing process is draft one, I'm just focused on finding my novelty, just the backbone of what makes anything interesting. And then draft two, I come back and try to increase the resonance by embedding story and analogy and examples. That's basically my process there.
turns.zh: 写作质量的本质是创新性乘以你让创新性在人们脑海中引发共鸣的叙事能力。我写作过程的结构是：初稿，我只专注于寻找创新性，找到让任何内容变得有趣的核心；然后在二稿，我回来试图通过嵌入故事、类比和例子来增强共鸣。这基本上就是我的流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that a lot. Just to add real quick, something I've learned is that if your stuff is really useful, it doesn't have to be written beautifully. A lot of people I think are afraid of writing because they think they have to write really well, like be real good writers. What I've learned is it's okay if you're not like. You just be good enough and you'll get better the more you do it. The most important thing is the content is valuable and interesting, which I think you're describing as novelty. I just want to make sure people don't get scared away and be like, "Oh my god, I need stories and metaphors and all these beautiful writing." Initially you don't is my experience, but it helps in a big way.
turns.zh: 我非常赞同这一点。事实上，我写作时最大的批评就是内容太干货，太注重新奇感，而缺乏共鸣感。但我特意这么做，是因为人们往往会过度追求共鸣感，反而让文章变得冗长。作为读者，我喜欢读简洁明了的文章，比如参考手册般的指南。我希望读到的内容要么是个人轶事，要么是人们生活中的真实故事，或者他们想与我分享的人生启示，又或者是纯粹的小说。各有所好嘛。你说得很到位。写作时要先想自己想读什么内容，这才是黄金法则。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I agree. In fact, the biggest criticism of my writing is that it is too dry, it's too novelty focused, and there's a lack of the resonance, but I do that purposely because oftentimes people can over-indulge in resonance and then it really bloats the piece. As a reader myself, I like reading super concise pieces, like reference manuals almost. I'm looking for the length from personal anecdotes, personal stories of people's lives or life lessons they've learned that they want to share with me, or actual fiction. To each their own. You're spot on. Do what you would want to read to me is the golden rule.
turns.zh: 我同意。事实上，对我写作最大的批评就是太干货，太注重新奇感，缺乏共鸣感，但我特意这么做，是因为人们往往会过度追求共鸣感，反而让文章变得冗长。作为读者，我喜欢读简洁明了的文章，比如参考手册般的指南。我在寻找个人轶事、人们生活中的真实故事，或者他们想与我分享的人生启示，或者纯粹的小说。各有所好嘛。你说得很到位。写作时要先想自己想读什么内容，这才是黄金法则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, and also don't be afraid. Don't feel like the bar's that high if you want to get started.
turns.zh: 太棒了，别害怕。如果你想开始写作，就别把标准定得太高。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: What have been your frameworks for sitting down and knowing that one of your newsletter editions is where you want it to be? And what do you think is the framework justifying that a piece is or explaining why a piece is good?
turns.zh: 你坐下来写作时，是如何确保某期通讯达到你期望的效果的？你认为怎样才能证明一篇文章质量高或者解释为什么一篇文章好？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The thing that I always strive for is this needs to be actionable and useful. It's something someone could take and do something with that day versus just a bunch of theory and pontification and philosophy. It's like, oh, here's a thing you can go do today.
turns.zh: 我一直追求的是内容要实用且有价值。读者拿起就能用，而不是一堆理论、空谈和哲学。这就像，哦，这里有件事你今天就能去实践。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: That's kind of my bar is make it very actionable, which I think is specific to the type of newsletter I have, not necessarily broad writing the way you're describing, but that's what I try.
turns.zh: 这就是我的标准——要确保内容实用且简洁，富有新意。不知道你是否也注意到了，要让内容真正实用，我必须给他们留一份速查表。因为如果有所有这些实用步骤，但它们分散在一期冗长的通讯里，让读者自己去整理一份速查表，形成一系列易于遵循的步骤，这实在太费脑力了。我觉得简化也是让内容实用的一个关键环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I agree with you, my rules of thumb are like it has to be actionable, concise, and novel. I'm not sure if you've seen this as well, but to make something truly actionable, I have to leave them with a cheat sheet. Because if I have all these actionable steps, but they're spread throughout a monster newsletter edition, it's too much mental work to go and make my own cheat sheet out of and have a quick to follow series of steps. I feel like compression is a key part of making something actionable as well.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这一点。我同意你的观点，写作的黄金法则是实用、简洁和新奇。我不确定你是否也注意到了，但要让内容真正实用，我必须给他们留一份速查表。因为如果有所有这些实用步骤，但它们分散在一期冗长的通讯里，让读者自己去整理一份速查表，形成一系列易于遵循的步骤，这实在太费脑力了。我觉得简化也是让内容实用的一个关键环节。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: There's a book called On Writing Well that taught me a lot about cutting two-thirds of what you've written to get to the core of it. I'm curious, what else are you doing to try to harden each newsletter edition to make sure it's good? Is it just like, hey, this is actionable and we were pretty comprehensive and I checked it past experts? Is that the extent of it, or what are you trying to do to feel like it's fantastic? What's your review process when you pass it by others as well?
turns.zh: 有一本书叫《写作的艺术》，它让我学到很多知识，比如如何删减三分之二的内容，直击核心。我很好奇，你还做了哪些工作来确保每期通讯质量上乘？是只是说，嘿，这很实用，我们做得很全面，我让专家检查过了吗？仅此而已吗？还是你还做了什么努力来让它变得出色？当你把作品交给别人评审时，你的评审流程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm happy to answer that, but I also know you got to run soon. I guess we could touch on... We could just save the fifth topic maybe for a follow up episode is one idea, or we could touch on it.
turns.zh: 我很乐意回答这个问题，但我也知道你马上要走了。我想我们可以先略过……或者把第五个话题留到下一期再谈，这都是可以的。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Sure. Up to you. Anything you want, my friend. If you want me to cover the next topic, super happy to. Up to you. Everyone listening right now is like, "Man, Julian's just been fucking rambling for an hour." I realized we were not having a conversation. Now I feel bad because I was so in my momentum of sharing some concepts that I didn't really have a conversation with.
turns.zh: 好的，随你便。朋友，你想聊什么都行。如果你想让我接下来讲下一个话题，我非常乐意。不过还是看你决定。现在听众肯定在想：“天啊，朱利安讲了一个小时废话。”我意识到我们根本没在真正对话。现在我感觉挺糟的，因为我太沉浸在分享观点中，完全没顾及交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is very normal for this podcast, so do not stress.
turns.zh: 这对这个播客来说很正常，别太在意。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: All right. Good. Actually, you should leave this all in here so they know I feel bad. I'm not cutting anything. What was the last topic again? Remind me.
turns.zh: 好的，没关系。实际上你应该把所有内容都保留在这里，好让听众知道我很内疚。我不会删掉任何内容。最后一个话题是什么来着？提醒我一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just saying, I think one of the things people really like about this podcast from what I hear often is they like that I'm not talking a lot. They kind of like that I'm letting the guests speak mostly, because a lot of podcast, the guest thinks they know at all, or sorry, the host and they just talk, talk, talk.
turns.zh: 我只是想说，据我常听到的，人们喜欢这个播客的原因之一就是我话不多。他们喜欢我让嘉宾多说话，因为很多播客里，嘉宾自以为很懂，或者对不起，是主持人一直在自说自话。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Oh, got you. The thing is you are brilliant. You're an actual host who is a useful, amazing human being and we want to hear your thoughts.
turns.zh: 哦，明白了。关键是你太棒了。你是个真正有用的、出色的主持人，我们都想听你的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was the last topic again?
turns.zh: 最后一个话题是什么？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: The last topic was the Creativity Faucet. We can save that for another talk, or if you want to touch on it, we can do that too.
turns.zh: 最后一个话题是“创造力水龙头”。我们可以留到下次再谈，或者如果你想提一下，也没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sure. Yeah, let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的，行吧。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: The quick version here is that this is an idea that I saw recur across three of the most prolific creators in the world, John Mayer, Ed Sheeran, Neil Gaiman. Ed Sheeran might work with other producers and so on, but the basic thing between the three is they're very independent creators who are constantly making blockbusters in large part on their own. I was curious, what on earth are those three doing that very few other people are doing? Taylor Swift also. One day I actually found the answer, what is their approach to consistently making phenomenal content? The way I found it was interesting.
turns.zh: 简单来说，这个概念在我观察到世界上三个最多产的创作者——约翰·梅尔、艾德·希兰、尼尔·盖曼身上反复出现。艾德·希兰可能和其他制作人合作等等，但这三人的共同点是他们都是非常独立的创作者，大部分爆款作品都是自己独立完成的。我很好奇，这三个人到底做了什么别人很少做的事？泰勒·斯威夫特也是。有一天我终于找到了答案，他们如何持续创作出惊艳内容的秘诀是什么？我找到的答案很有趣。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I was watching a masterclass, like Masterclass.com, with Neil Gaman and he explained his process for writing fiction novels. And then in the same year, I watched the documentary of Ed Sheeran explaining his process for writing songs and they were identical. And then a year later, I came across a YouTube video that I posted on Twitter with John Mayer spinning his process, also identical. I'm like, fuck, there's the answer. They don't have a name for their process, so I just call it the Creativity Faucet. Very quickly, what they do is they visualize their creativity as a backed up pipe of water. The first mile is packed with wastewater, and this wastewater has to be emptied before the clear water behind it can arrive.
turns.zh: 我在Masterclass.com上听尼尔·盖曼讲解小说写作过程。同年，我看了艾德·希兰的纪录片，里面他解释歌曲创作过程，两者如出一辙。一年后，我又刷到约翰·梅尔在YouTube上分享创作心得，方法也完全一致。我当时想，天啊，这就是答案。他们对自己的创作过程没有特定名称，所以我把它称为创造力水龙头。简单来说，他们的做法是把创造力想象成一根被堵塞的水管。第一英里是堆积的污水，而这些污水必须先排空，后面清澈的水才能流出来。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Because your creativity pipe or Creativity Faucet only has one faucet, there's no shortcut to achieving the clarity, the clear water of good ideas, until you first empty the wastewater out. If we apply that to creativity at the beginning of every writing session, write out every bad idea that comes to mind. Instead of being self-critical and resisting these bad ideas, you have to recognize bad ideas is progress. Because once they are emptied out of you, the better ideas begin to arrive. Here's the key part, why do good ideas arrive after the bad ideas are empty? It's because when you've gone through a bunch of bad ideas, your brain, your mind starts reflexively identifying what elements are causing the badness.
turns.zh: 由于你的创意管道或“创意水龙头”只有一个出口，要想获得清晰的思路和好点子，就必须先把阻塞物清理掉。如果我们把这个道理应用到写作前的创意准备阶段，写下脑海中浮现的每一个糟糕点子。不要自我批评或抗拒这些坏点子，而是要认识到坏点子也是进步的标志。因为一旦把它们排除后，更好的创意就会涌现。这里有个关键点：为什么好点子要在坏点子被清除后才会出现？因为当你经历了一系列坏点子后，大脑会开始自动识别导致这些坏点子的元素。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: Then it becomes way better at avoiding those bad elements and you become way better at pattern matching the novel ideas with way greater intuition. Most creators are resisting their bad ideas. If you sat down, scribbled a few thoughts in a blank document, and just walked away because you weren't struck with gold, then you never actually finished the creative process. There's no way you would've come up with gold. Like Neil and Ed, for example, they know they're not superhuman. What they're doing is in every creative session, they simply have the discipline to allot time no matter how long it takes, it could be an hour, to empty all of the bad ideas.
turns.zh: 然后你就能更有效地避开这些负面元素，并以更强的直觉匹配新奇的创意。大多数创作者都在抗拒自己的坏点子。如果你坐在空白文档前，随便写下几个想法，然后因为没有灵感就放弃，那你就从未真正完成过创作过程。这样根本不可能产生灵感的火花。比如尼尔和埃德，他们深知自己并非超人。他们在每次创作时，都会坚持无论花多长时间（哪怕一小时）都坚持排空所有坏点子。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: And then they're not worried about whether good ideas will come after the bad ones because they know the following process. You start with a weak imitation. You identify what makes your invitation weak, and then you iterate the imitation until it's finally original. And that is the process you have to just throw yourself into.
turns.zh: 然后他们不再担忧好点子是否会在坏点子之后出现，因为他们深知后续的流程。首先从一个弱模仿开始，识别出邀请函的弱点，然后不断迭代模仿，直到最终形成原创。这就是你必须全身心投入的流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I feel like I don't do that enough. I feel like when I get to writing, I'm just like, "Okay, let's make this awesome." This is a really good reminder just to get stuff out. It connects to the concept of the shitty first draft. Just write. It'll be bad. And then you edit. You asked me this question, what my process is for writing, and most of it is just refining like a thousand times. I just kind of take a first pass and then I look at it, make it better, look at it, make it better, and just kind of keep editing for days and days and days until it's not bad.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个理念。我觉得自己做得不够。比如开始写作时，我总会想：“好吧，让它变得超棒。”这真是个很好的提醒，要先把东西写出来，再慢慢完善。正如你问我的创作流程，我大部分时间都在反复润色。先写一稿，再审视，改进，再审视，再改进，这样反复数日直到满意为止。

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
turns.en: I love that. That's what I've always done, until one day I was like, "I need a process here." Anyway dude, pleasure chatting. You're a gent. Sorry to all the listeners for rambling so much at a high pace. Cut anything you want. You can cut all of that. I don't care. Whatever you find interesting, go with. We're just going to have this final goodbye and that's it.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这种方法。直到有一天我意识到：“我需要一个固定流程。”总之，聊得很开心，你人真好。抱歉给听众讲了这么多废话。想剪掉什么就剪吧，全剪掉也无妨。只要你们觉得有意思就行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was very anti-climactic. Cool, man. Where can folks find you online and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 这结尾太平淡了。不错，伙计。听众在哪里能找到你？怎么能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Julian Shapiro
